Guided Inquiry

Predict before you run it

You are about to close the switch on a battery, resistor and empty capacitor in series. When is the current through the resistor largest?

One clock, two quantities

VC climbs steeply, then crawls. I falls steeply from its t = 0 maximum, then crawls. Neither is a straight line: the approach is exponential.

They are locked together, because the resistor only sees the part of the supply the capacitor has not taken yet: I = (Vsupply − VC) / R. So VC/Vsupply and I/I0 sum to 1.

Different units, different scales: volts on the blue left axis, milliamps on the amber right axis.

The circuit's own clock

τ = RC is the only quantity that sets how fast this happens. The pink cross-hair marks it: a vertical at t = τ, a horizontal at 63.2% of the supply, meeting on the VC curve.

Raising R or C raises τ and stretches the curve along the time axis; lowering either squashes it. The shape never changes, and the meeting point never leaves the curve: at one time constant the capacitor has always covered 63.2% of the gap to its final voltage.

Discharging — same fraction, other direction

Now the capacitor starts fully charged, the battery is switched out, and it drains through R. At t = τ, what fraction of the supply does VC read?

The one thing to keep

At one time constant the capacitor has covered 63.2% of the gap to its final voltage — charging or discharging, for every R and every C. By 5τ it is more than 99% of the way there, which is why 5τ is quoted as the practical settling time.

And the current decays exponentially in both directions. It never builds: it is largest the instant the switch moves, in charging and in discharging alike.

01

At a glance

A battery, a resistor and a capacitor share one loop, and the sim draws the capacitor voltage and the current against one clock as the switch moves. Charging and discharging an RC circuit is the model behind every timing delay, flash and filter built from these two parts.

What you'll learn

  • How the capacitor voltage and the current change with time after the switch moves.
  • Which quantity sets how fast the change happens, and how R and C enter it.
  • How charging and discharging compare, and how long the circuit takes to settle.
One loop: the same current passes through the battery, resistor and capacitor in turn.

What's on screen

  • Circuit (left): battery, switch labelled charge or discharge, R, an ammeter in mA, and the capacitor with its + and − plate charges.
  • Blue curve: the capacitor voltage VC, read on the left axis in volts.
  • Amber curve: the current I, read on the right axis in mA. The time axis is fixed at 0 to 20 ms.
  • Pink cross-hair: marks the circuit's own time scale τ on the curve.
  • Live readouts: VC, I, τ, the time t, and the share of the gap covered.
See itClose the switch on an empty capacitor with R = 1.0 kΩ and C = 2.0 μF. Watch for: the blue and amber traces drawing left to right while the readouts change.

03

The resistor sees only the gap the capacitor has left

In one loop the supply voltage splits between the resistor and the capacitor: Vsupply = IR + VC. So the current depends on the gap, the part of the supply the capacitor has not taken yet:

I = (Vsupply − VC) / R
The resistor carries whatever voltage the capacitor does not.

At the instant the switch closes the capacitor is empty, VC = 0, so the resistor sees all 12 V and I = 12 V / 1.0 kΩ = 12 mA. That is the largest the current ever gets: an empty capacitor acts like a plain wire. As VC rises, the gap shrinks and I falls with it.

See itCharge from empty with R = 1.0 kΩ and C = 2.0 μF. Watch for: I opening at 12.00 mA while VC opens at 0.00 V, then VC rising as I falls.
04

Both curves are exponentials, locked together

The gap sets the current, and the current is what shrinks the gap, so each is always a fixed fraction of its own earlier size. That is an exponential, with τ a time fixed by the circuit:

VC(t) = Vsupply(1 − e−t/τ)
I(t) = I0 e−t/τ,   I0 = Vsupply / R
Neither curve is a straight line.

The two are locked: VC/Vsupply + I/I0 = 1 at every moment. VC climbs steeply, then crawls; I falls steeply, then crawls. The gap halves every 0.693 τ, so with τ = 1.00 ms the capacitor reaches half the supply at 0.69 ms, and the current has fallen to half of I0 at that same instant.

See itFreeze a charging run with R = 1.0 kΩ and C = 1.0 μF at t = 0.69 ms. Watch for: VC at 6.00 V and I at 6.00 mA, each half of its limit.
05

The time constant τ = RC sets the pace

The circuit's own clock is the product of its two parts:

τ = RC  ⟹  VC(τ) = 0.632 Vsupply
With R in kΩ and C in μF, τ comes out in ms.

A larger R lets less current through, and a larger C needs more charge to reach the same voltage, so either one raises τ and stretches both curves along the time axis. The shape never changes. After one time constant the capacitor has covered 63.2% of the gap to its final voltage (1 − 1/e), for every R and every C. With R = 2.0 kΩ and C = 1.5 μF, τ = 3.00 ms and VC(τ) = 7.59 V.

See itFreeze a charging run with R = 2.0 kΩ and C = 1.5 μF at t = τ. Watch for: the pink cross-hair meeting the blue curve at 3.00 ms, with the gap covered reading 63.2%.
06

Discharging runs the same law in the other direction

On Discharge the battery is switched out and the full capacitor drains through R alone. With V0 the voltage it starts from (12 V here):

VC(t) = V0 e−t/τ
|I(t)| = (V0/R) e−t/τ
The same τ = RC, the same 63.2% of the gap.

The gap is now V0 itself, so after τ the capacitor has covered 63.2% of it and 36.8% remains: VC(τ) = 0.368 × 12 V = 4.41 V. The sim's "gap covered" readout therefore reads 63.2% while VC is at 36.8% of the supply. The current again peaks the instant the switch moves, 12 mA here, and then decays the same way, but it runs the opposite way round the loop.

See itFreeze a discharge with R = 1.0 kΩ and C = 1.0 μF at t = τ. Watch for: VC at 4.41 V, the label battery switched out, and 63.2% in the gap covered.
07

Five time constants settle it for practical purposes

The curve never reaches its final value exactly. After n time constants the gap left is e−n of what it began as:

timegap coveredgap left
1 τ63.2%36.8%
2 τ86.5%13.5%
3 τ95.0%5.0%
5 τ99.3%0.7%

By 5τ the capacitor is more than 99% of the way, which is why 5τ is quoted as the settling time. With τ = 1.00 ms, 5τ is 5.00 ms and VC = 11.92 V, only 0.08 V short of 12 V. If τ is above 4 ms, 5τ lies beyond the 20 ms axis, so the plot shows only part of the settling.

See itFreeze a charging run with R = 1.0 kΩ and C = 1.0 μF at t = 5τ. Watch for: VC at 11.92 V and the gap covered at 99.3%.
08

Where it matters

  • Timing and delay. A circuit that waits until VC reaches a chosen level takes a time proportional to RC. Choosing R and C sets the delay of a flasher or a timer chip.
  • Camera flash. A capacitor charges slowly through a large resistance, then discharges through the lamp, whose resistance is small, so τ is short and the energy leaves in a quick burst.
  • Smoothing. A capacitor across a rectified supply discharges into the load with τ = RC. If RC is long compared with the ripple period, VC barely sags between peaks.
09

Summary

In one line. After the switch moves, the current and the capacitor voltage change exponentially on one clock, τ = RC.

Key points

  • I = (Vsupply − VC)/R, so I is largest the instant the switch moves.
  • At t = τ the capacitor has covered 63.2% of the gap, charging or discharging, for any R and C.
  • 5τ is the practical settling time: more than 99% of the gap is covered.

Common mix-ups

  • "The capacitor fills at a steady rate, so the current builds up." The current is largest at the start and falls as VC rises.
  • "τ is the time to charge fully." At τ the capacitor is 63.2% of the way. It never arrives exactly, and 5τ is the practical estimate.
  • "A bigger R makes the capacitor end at a lower voltage." The final VC is 12 V for any R. R only changes how long it takes.

Things to try on your own

  • Run R = 2.0 kΩ with C = 1.0 μF, then R = 1.0 kΩ with C = 2.0 μF. Compare the blue curves and where each amber curve starts.
  • Find R and C that give τ = 4.0 ms, and read VC at t = 4.0 ms.
  • Set R = 0.2 kΩ and watch the amber curve start at the top of its scale.
